subject: English
passage: The Leopard is a 1958 novel by Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa. Although Prince Fabrizio has been politically outmaneuvered by the rising bourgeois faction led by Don Calogero, he intimates that he is not entirely ready to yield his authority to the new order, saying, ______
prompt: Which quotation from The Leopard most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: "So be it, then. Long live the new men! Let them govern as they will; I am no longer among their number, and ask only to be forgotten in my own halls."
choices.B: "What am I now—neither prince nor peasant, stripped of the name my fathers bore, wandering through rooms that no longer know me, uncertain by what title I should answer when summoned?"
choices.C: "They may take my estates, my titles, the very walls of this palace; but the memory of what we were is mine alone, and over that kingdom no Calogero shall ever reign."
choices.D: "Why must I be called so soon to pay my respects, before I have set aside the habits of command in which I was reared? I have scarcely yet learned to defer, to flatter, to incline my head before lesser men."

explanation:
Choice D is the best answer because it most effectively illustrates the claim that Prince Fabrizio intimates he is not entirely ready to yield his authority to the new order. In the quotation, Fabrizio explicitly states that he has not yet 'set aside the habits of command' in which he was reared, suggesting he still thinks of himself as a figure of authority. Furthermore, he says he has 'scarcely yet learned to defer, to flatter, to incline my head before lesser men'—actions that would demonstrate submission to Don Calogero and the new political order. By stating that he hasn't learned these behaviors, Fabrizio is indicating that he is not yet ready to be submissive, despite having been politically outmaneuvered.

Why C is incorrect:

Choice C is incorrect because although the quotation does show Fabrizio asserting a form of defiance, it doesn't address his readiness to yield authority. He claims that while his adversaries may take his estates and titles, they cannot take the memory of his family's legacy, over which he remains sovereign. This is about Fabrizio maintaining ownership of memory, not about his willingness or unwillingness to perform acts of submission to Don Calogero.
